structure: Single-grade Vermont draft framework document (Grade 8 - Civics and Economics in Action). Front matter: header banner, title/theme, Overview narrative, Looking Back/Looking Ahead, Inquiry rationale and contact. Inquiry Process block: 'Inquiry Process (K-12)' statement, a banded list of C3 indicators (6-8) and overarching grade themes. Body is organized by four subject sections (Civics, Economics, Geography, History), each with a 'Theme:' line, C3-strand headings (e.g. Civic and Political Institutions; Economic Decision Making; Geographic Representations; Change, Continuity, and Context) followed by the C3 indicator codes (D2.<Dim>.<n>.6-8). Each strand/indicator group is followed by a 2-column table (R1 headers 'Sample C3 Indicator Connections' | 'Sample Content Connections'; R2 cells hold C1 = 'Students will...' expectations, C2 = bulleted sample content). Rows continued over pages start with 'Continue'. Each subject ends with a 'Resources' list of suggested lessons/inquiries (C3 IDM, iCivics, PBS, etc.). The vermont.gov banner and running headers are furniture. No state-specific standard codes; the D2 C3 codes and the 'Students will' expectations are the standards. Labeling: titles/themes/strand headings/codes/inquiry indicators/'Students will' cells = standards; Sample Content Connections cells, Overview narrative and Resources = examples; Looking Back/Ahead, inquiry rationale, scope notes = backup.
issues: Inquiry Process / C3-indicator / Priority Performance Indicator lists that name a band (K-2, 3-5, 6-8) or K-12 are labeled with that band (shared inquiry skills); everything else is labeled with this file's single grade, per the state guide (one document = one grade).
Resource entries that wrap across pages are split into two units (second unit continues the first); both are labeled examples.
'Note:' lines saying an indicator is not addressed in this grade, and the 'Looking Back/Looking Ahead' paragraphs, are labeled backup.
u21-u23: 'Note: Free Civics Curricula' lists suggested free curricula before the Civics section; labeled examples.
u92: note says Economic Decision Making indicators are not in grade 8; labeled backup.
History tables are numbered T1/T2 on the same page (e.g. u144-u147 and u157-u160); handled by cell position.
u122, u165: 'Continue' prefix in C1 expectation cells; labeled standards.
u18: overarching themes list 'Geography (in grades 6 and 7)' although grade 8 has no Geography section; labeled grade 8 standards.

Grade 8 – Civics and Economics in Action (Draft)
Overview

In grade 8, students will utilize past knowledge and understanding to expand their focus on the core concepts and principles underlying America’s democracy; the structure and limits of the national government as set forth in the United States Constitution, including an examination of democratic ideals; and the role of the citizen in a democratic society. Students will collaborate to identify a problem(s); develop solutions that would require government involvement; and participate in student-led civics projects focused on developing civic knowledge, skills, dispositions, and media literacy. Students will also learn about the workings of local, national, and global economies and develop an understanding of the decision-making processes of individuals, businesses, and governments and how they are connected. Gaining an understanding of economic resources, such as human capital, land, technology, and investments, and how they play a role in big-picture decision making in a global environment will assist students in making informed decisions in a wide variety of contexts.
Looking Back

In grade 7, students built on their knowledge of Vermont and United States politics, geography, economics, and history as they re-visited the sectional conflicts over slavery that continued into Reconstruction and beyond and led to the long struggle in the 19th and 20th centuries for civil rights.
Inquiry

Why inquiry? Using inquiry as an instructional model for the teaching of social studies allows students to authentically ask questions, search for and analyze evidence, and provide explanations and arguments to challenges facing their world.
Contact: Martha Deiss, Curriculum & Instruction Division, at Martha.Deiss@vermont.gov

The inquiry instructional model is driven by authentic questions or problems that have relevance for children. Students learn content, skills, and dispositions as they seek answers to questions and as they apply their learning to take informed action. Pioneered by Dewey (1938), inquiry is an attempt to make classroom experiences feel more like the authentic, curiosity-driven experiences that motivate learning outside of school. (Using Inquiry to Prepare Students for College, Career, and Civic Life, elementary edition, p. 22)

The Inquiry Arc is defined in Dimension 1 (questioning) of the College, Career, and Civic Life (C3) Framework for Social Studies State Standards. In this Framework, Dimension 3 (evidence sourcing), and Dimension 4 (communicating), as well as some evidence indicators found within Dimension 2 – History, have been combined with Dimension 1 into a singular Inquiry Process, as evidenced below. This Inquiry Process begins in the elementary grades and increases in depth and complexity as it spans through high school, preparing students to spiral their learning and skill acquisition in the social studies for college and career readiness.
Inquiry Process (K-12): Students act as social scientists as they ask questions, think critically, solve problems, and share conclusions.
C3 Indicators (6-8):
Constructing Compelling and Supporting Questions: D1.1, 2, 3; His. 12
Gathering and Evaluating Sources: D2. His. 6, 10, 12, 13; D3. 1, 2, 3
Communicating and Critiquing Conclusions: D2. His. 16; D4. 1, 2, 4
Overarching Themes:
• Foundations and Roles • Economics and Policy • Geography (in grades 6 and 7) • Civic Participation in a Democracy

Certain Unalienable Rights - National Archives: Students will explore the Declaration of Independence as an artifact, a primary source, and a persuasive text. Students explore the document’s important sections and evaluate the persuasive elements of the Declaration of Independence. This Civics for All of US distance learning program is available for groups of 10 or more students free of charge. Each program will be led by one of our educators located at National Archives sites, the Center for Legislative Archives, and Presidential Libraries across the country. After submitting your program request, you will be connected to an available National Archives educator to confirm your reservation. We require that the

Programs are also offered as regularly scheduled interactive webinars. Registration is required, but there is no minimum attendance prerequisite.

Civics and Government - PBS Learning Media: Search interactive lessons, videos, and other PBS-related resources within the Topic Area of The American Political System to find resources in “American Documents,” “American Identity and Diversity,” “American Laws and Rights,” and "The Practice of American Citizenship,” among others.

Democracy in Dialogue Virtual Exchange Program - Smithsonian Institute: Become a Smithsonian Virtual Exchange Facilitator and learn how to collaboratively design and lead place-based investigations with your students to better understand the stories emanating from your hometown. Share and reflect with another community in another corner of the country. Celebrate the commonalities and the differences.
Educator Resources - Educating for American Democracy: A clearinghouse for vetted resources; search by grade- level, topic, resource-type.

Explore the Declaration of Independence - PBS Learning Media: In this interactive lesson, students are guided through a close reading and analysis of the Declaration of Independence, one of the nation’s founding documents. The lesson highlights the Declaration of Independence’s historical context, its Enlightenment influences, and its elevation to one of a handful of revered documents in U.S. history.

Exploring Local Government - PBS Learning Media: With this interactive image, students can discover the vital role that town government plays in shaping the community and impacting the daily lives of its residents. Explore various town departments and learn how they provide essential services, maintain infrastructure, and ensure public safety. When you understand the roles of town departments, you are more likely to be able to change or have an impact on your community. Also included are teaching tips, discussion questions, and an independent student activity.
Freedom and Unity - The Center for Cartoon Studies: A downloadable version of the Center’s “Graphic Guide to Civics and Democracy in Vermont.”

Getting to Know Your Neighbor - Statistics in Schools: Suggested for grades 5,6 but can used for students to learn more about their community when they research public policy issues. To introduce demographic characteristics to students, teachers will help them create a population pyramid. Then, students will use an online tool called QuickFacts to find census data on demographic characteristics for a county in 2024. They will compare it to older data from the same county to find changes and trends over time. They will then use QuickFacts to examine data about their school’s county.

International Affairs - iCivics: Students learn about the complex interactions that exist in our globalized world. They examine the evolution of diplomacy and international interdependence by looking at recent and historical global events.

Multiple Grade 7-8 lessons on the Constitution - Center for Civic Education: Lessons adapted from the We the People Level 2 text, with lesson purpose, objectives, terms to understand, readings, supplemental sources, and activities. Lessons include: “What is the Federal System Created by the Constitution?”, “Why do We Need a Government?”, and “How Can Citizens participate?”, among others.

The Constitution - iCivics: Students will learn how our Constitution was created and what some of its key characteristics are. They will also explore key amendments to the Constitution and their application in protecting citizens' rights.
The Resource Center - Center for Civic Education: Free resources including curricular crosswalks, lesson plans, online courses, “60-Second Daily Podcast” and “The Constitution EXPLAINED” videos.

This is What Democracy Looks Like - The Center for Cartoon Studies: Download this 32-page comic book that explains what democracy actually means and how the whole thing works. Vermont Classroom Blueprint - Vermont Office of the Secretary of State: A K-12 ‘blueprint’ providing resources and lesson plans for active civic engagement in your classroom.

Resources

Analyzing Correlations Between Education and Income - Statistics in Schools: Students will explore maps containing census data from 1950 through 2000. They will analyze how education levels and median household incomes have changed over time and determine how the two might be correlated. Students will also come up with ideas for policies that could help address issues related to income and education.

Fiscal Policy and Monetary Policy: What’s the Difference? - Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond: Activities and lesson plans for students to understand the policy differences and the role of the Federal Reserve in influencing the economy.

Illicit: The Dark Trade - National Geographic: Resources are unevenly distributed across the surface of the Earth, and no one country has all the resources it needs. Therefore, each country must trade with others, resulting in a world of global economic interdependence—an exchange between “producers” (those who produce or manufacture goods) and “consumers” (those who purchase or use the goods). The two following activities help students understand the concept of economic interdependence between different countries, and understand terms such as trade, import, and export. A trading simulation will help students understand the conditions that encourage or discourage trade among countries. In
Grade 8 - Civics and Economics in Action (Draft) (Revised: November 12, 2025)
Page 13 of 18

the activities, students will split into country groups and employ product-unit trading cards to represent the net worth of five world countries. They will use these trading cards to obtain goods not available in their country and to disperse goods that their country produces. Students will discover that some commodities are more desirable than others and that shifts in an economic market can directly affect the price of goods.

The Federal Reserve and You - Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia: In this lesson, students view a film segment from The Federal Reserve and You that introduces the Federal Reserve. Using an anticipation/reaction guide, students learn what the Fed is, what it does, and what its impact on the economy is.
The Story of Monetary Policy - Federal Reserve Bank of New York: This lesson plan allows students to discuss the ways in which monetary policy can help reduce periods of economic sickness.

Where Should I Live? Using U.S. Census Bureau Data to Make Decisions - Statistics in Schools: Students can use this lesson as a means to learn and interpret data when they are considering their public policy. Students will use the U.S. Census Bureau’s QuickFacts data access tool to examine information about three cities, including population, education, and income data. Students will draw conclusions about life in those three cities to determine which city they would like to live in as an adult.
Why We Pay Taxes - NextGen Personal Finance: This unit 3, lesson 4 lesson helps students understand fiscal policy as they analyze why federal taxes are removed from their paycheck.
